Not really, mechanical playback devices are lossy. It's like saving text as JPEG over and over again, except here it's written once (like cd-r) and every playback is like the JPEG's over and over again. Just ignoring the data degradation, assuming the data rate to be something like 20kbps or and assuming a length of 60 minute per cassette, each cassette would hold just about 9MB, or a little over 10MB for the 70 minute cassette. So, it would take almost seven minutes to store just a megabyte (assuming writing could be done as fast-slow as reading). You'd need 13 million of these cassettes to just store as much data as a 128GB uSD card, or probably twice or triple that, because it's lossy data and you'd need several copies for redundancy. So, to store the fingernail-sided SD-card nucrear-war-proof, you need to place it in a box sturdy enogh, let's say a 10x10x10cm steel cube. To store millions of these cartridges nuclear-proof, you'd need some underground bunker big enough to evacuate a small city.
Oh, and to store that 128GB of data on 13 million of these, it'd take about 1500 years.

Lots of people talk about gateway games - games that are considered modern hobby board games with more strategy or more tactical thinking than say Monopoly or Sorry.

What games have you successfully used (or played yourself) to bring more folks into the hobby? What game got you into modern board gaming?
Talk to us about 'gateway' games. What games would you use to bring different people into the hobby?

Believe it or not, I've used Talisman as a gateway game.

My wife was very familiar with Monopoly type games and wanted to participate with us in our gaming group. I had just received the 4th edition Black Isle version of Talisman a week before, so we gave it a go.

She loved it! She's already familiar with roll and move, the combat system is about as simplistic as it could be and the rest fell into place for her in the first 15 minutes of the (admittedly long) game.

She's now a full fledged gamer and often beats the snot out of me at games like Splendor or Star Realms, or Seasons. Or just about most of the games I own. What have I done?!

The two I've played with new folks that seem to work fairly well are Munchkin and Settlers. They're both simple rules-wise but require some higher level strategy. Munchkin in particular requires that folks interact and get involved. That tends to help.
I was coming here to say these two games. I recently added the card games mile Bourne and conquest of orion to my list
Carcasson, Catan, & Munchkin are my 3 go to games for new people.

Somehow I stumbled upon Tabletop a couple of summers ago. I don't know how I got there but I do know I spent hours watching all that I could of it until I fell asleep. I wanted so many tabletop games after binging that series. The one I had to get first was Ticket to Ride. Smallworld shortly after that. TTR was certainly my gateway as I am now loaded with board games. It's usually the first one I suggest when I introduce friends to modern board gaming.
Dice masters. So easy and cheap. for 25 dollars in a storeyou will get a starter that 2 people can play with and 20 extra cards with the dice.

It's a bit of a lame response at this time but I strongly encourage folks to use the list of games played on Tabletop. Their selection criteria are perfect for new gamers as they look for games that are relatively easy to teach and learn, have interesting and high quality artwork/themes, generally don't have any player-elimination mechanics that knock someone out of the game completely before it's over.

Obviously some are more complex than others but I don't think you can go wrong with most anything they've played on the show, especially the earlier episodes where they hit the newer "classics" like Ticket To Ride, Carcassonne, etc.

The first few things I played when i joined a regular game night: Tiny Epic Defenders and Tiny Epic Kingdom, Elysium, DC Deckbuilder, Dead of Winter (not a gateway game). Also a game that two of the regulars made called Quest Board, but that's not available yet

Ticket to Ride - The rules are simple to learn and shows that there are different mechanics than simple roll and move.

Carcassonne This game introduces tile placement with easy to learn rules. Simple yet strategic.

Times Up / Dixit / Snake Oil There are more of party games but they help bring in some new players to the circle. We bring one of these out for those who are intimidated by games with too much strategy.

King of Tokyo This game introduces direct conflict. Some players love it, some do not. I use this to judge if my new players like conflict. If they do, try Small World. Personally, I hate conflict and never attack. To each their own.

Takenoko I use the cute panda and artwork to lure in parents and others who will adore the cute art. It looks like a children's game but actually has strategy, depth and replayability.

Resistance If the people you are trying to bring into gaming are outgoing, this is a great game. Sometimes, it doesn't go well with introverts or shy players. The louder, the better.
